source_text: Εἰ δὲ θέλεις αὐτοῦ καταμαθεῖν τὴν ἀρετὴν, ἔπελθε τῶν μελῶν ἁπάντων τὴν διάπλασιν, τὸ σχῆμα, τὰς ἐνεργείας, τὴν πρὸς ἄλληλα συμφωνίαν· καὶ πάσης πόλεως εὐνομουμένης καὶ φιλοσόφους ἅπαντας τοὺς πολίτας ἐχούσης ἀκριβεστέραν ὄψει τὴν τῶν μελῶν τούτων πρὸς ἄλληλα πολιτείαν. Εἰ δὲ ἄνω καὶ κάτω ταῦτα παρατρέχων, τὸ φθαρτὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ θνητὸν μόνον προτείνοις, οὐδὲ ἐντεῦθεν ἀπορήσομεν ἀπολογίας. Ὅτι γὰρ οὐ μόνον οὐδεμία γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ἡ βλάβη, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολὺ τὸ κέρδος τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων, δῆλον ἐκεῖθεν. Οἵ τε γὰρ ἅγιοι πάντες μετὰ τούτου ζῶντες, τὴν ἀγγελικὴν ἐκείνην ἐπεδείξαντο πολιτείαν, καὶ οὐδεμία τις αὐτοῖς ἐντεῦθεν ἐγίνετο βλάβη πρὸς τὸν τῆς ἀρετῆς δρόμον· οἵ τε πρὸς ἀσέβειαν βλέποντες οὐ μικρὸν ἔσχον κώλυμα, τοῦ σώματος τὴν φθορὰν, πρὸς τὸ μὴ ποῤῥωτέρω προελθεῖν τῆς οἰκείας παρανομίας. Εἰ γὰρ τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο καὶ παθητὸν σῶμα περικείμενοι πολλοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἰσοθεΐαν ἐφαντάσθησαν, καὶ ὑπὲρ τοῦ τοιαύτην ἑαυτοῖς περιθεῖναι δόξαν πολλὰ ἐπραγματεύσαντο· εἰ μὴ παθητὸν εἶχον τὸ σῶμα καὶ φθαρτὸν, ἐλέγχον αὐτῶν τὴν ἀσθένειαν, τίνας οὐκ ἂν ἠπάτησαν τῶν ἀνοητοτέρων; Ὅταν οὖν καὶ ἀσεβείας, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἔσχατος ὅρος κακίας, κώλυμα φαίνηται γινόμενον, καὶ τοῖς ἁγίοις παρέχῃ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἀνδρείαν ἐπιδείκνυσθαι, τίνος ἂν τύχοιεν συγγνώμης οἱ διαβάλλοντες αὐτὸ καὶ κακίζοντες; Οὐ γὰρ δὴ ταῦτα ἂν ἔχοιμεν περὶ αὐτοῦ μόνα εἰπεῖν, ἀλλ' ὅτι καὶ θεογνωσίας ἡμῖν αἴτιον γέγονεν αὐτό. Εἰ γὰρ τὰ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται, καὶ ἡ πίστις ἐξ ἀκοῆς, εὔδηλον ὅτι δι' ὀφθαλμῶν καὶ ὤτων χειραγωγηθεῖσα ἡ ψυχὴ τὸν ποιήσαντα αὐτὴν ἐπέγνω Θεόν. Διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸ φιλεῖ Παῦλος, καὶ βοᾷ λέγων, ὅτι Οὐ θέλομεν αὐτὸ ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι αὐτῷ τὴν ἀθανασίαν. Καὶ μή μοι λέγε· Πῶς δύναται ἀναστῆναι τὸ σῶμα πάλιν καὶ γενέσθαι ἄφθαρτον; Ὅταν γὰρ ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ δύναμις ἐργάζηται, τὸ πῶς μὴ προσκείσθω. Καὶ τί λέγω ἐπὶ Θεοῦ; Σὲ δημιουργὸν αὐτὸν ἐποίησεν ἀναστάσεως γενέσθαι, τοῦτο μὲν ἐπὶ τῶν σπερμάτων, τοῦτο δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν τεχνῶν, τοῦτο δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν ὑλῶν τῶν μεταλλικῶν. Καὶ γὰρ τὰ σπέρματα ἂν μὴ πρότερον ἀποθάνῃ καὶ σαπῇ καὶ διαφθαρῇ, οὐ τίκτει τὸν ἄσταχυν. Ὥσπερ οὖν ὁρῶν ἐκεῖ τὸν κόκκον σηπόμενον καὶ διαλυόμενον, οὐκ ἀμφιβάλλεις περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως, ἀλλ' ἀπόδειξιν σαυτοῦ ποιεῖσαι σαφεστάτην· ἂν γὰρ μὴ μείνῃ σηπόμενος μηδὲ φθειρόμενος, οὐκ ἂν ἀνασταίη ποτέ· οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ σώματος λογίζου τοῦ σοῦ· ὅταν ἴδῃς τὴν φθορὰν, τότε μάλιστα περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως φιλοσόφει. Ὁ γὰρ θάνατος οὐδὲν ἕτερόν ἐστιν, ἢ τῆς φθορᾶς λοιπὸν ἀναίρεσις· οὐ γὰρ δὴ τὸ σῶμα ἁπλῶς, ἀλλὰ τὴν φθορὰν αὐτοῦ δαπανᾷ ὁ θάνατος. Τοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν μεταλλικῶν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ὑλῶν συμβαῖνον. Τὴν γοῦν χρυσῖτιν γῆν λαμβάνουσιν οἱ περὶ ταῦτα ἔμπειροι, καὶ τῷ χωνευτηρίῳ παραδιδόντες χρυσίον ἐργάζονται, καὶ ἄμμον καὶ ἑτέραν ὕλην ἀναμιγνύντες, ὕελον καθαρὸν ἐποίησαν. Εἶτα ὅπερ ἡ τοῦ πυρὸς δύναμις, τοῦτο ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐ δυνήσεται χάρις, εἰπέ μοι; καὶ τίς ἂν ταῦτα εἴποι τῶν ὁπωσοῦν νοῦν ἐχόντων; Πῶς σε παρὰ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐποίησεν, ἐννόησον, καὶ μηκέτι ἀμφίβαλλε περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως.
thought_title: The body's excellence and corruption as a curb on evil
orientation: Chrysostom is defending the body against its accusers, arguing that its corruption is not a defect but a benefit, and that God's power makes resurrection credible.
pass_a_gloss: But if you wish to learn its virtue, go through the formation of all the members, the shape, the activities, the harmony toward one another; and you will see a constitution of these members toward one another more exact than every well-governed city and than a city having all its citizens philosophers. But if you run past these things up and down, and put forward only its corruptible and mortal aspect, not even from there will we lack a defense. For that not only no harm has come from there, but also much gain to the race of humans, is clear from there. For all the saints, living with this body, displayed that angelic way of life, and no harm came to them from there toward the course of virtue; and those looking toward impiety had no small hindrance, the corruption of the body, toward not advancing further in their own lawlessness. For if, wearing this corruptible and passible body, many humans imagined equality with God, and for the sake of putting such glory around themselves they did many things; if they did not have a passible and corruptible body, refuting their weakness, whom would they not have deceived among the more foolish? When therefore it appears to become a hindrance even of impiety, which is the furthest limit of wickedness, and provides for the saints to display the courage of the soul, what pardon would those obtain who slander it and abuse it? For we would not be able to say only these things about it, but that it has also become for us a cause of knowledge of God. For if his invisible things are clearly seen, being understood from the creation of the world by the things made, and faith comes from hearing, it is very clear that the soul, led by the hand through eyes and ears, recognized God who made it. Because of this very thing Paul loves it, and cries out saying, that We do not wish to strip it off, but to put on over it immortality. And do not tell me: How can the body rise again and become incorruptible? For when the power of God is at work, let the how not be added. And why do I speak about God? He made you yourself a craftsman of resurrection, on the one hand in seeds, on the other hand in crafts, and on the other hand in metallic materials. For seeds, unless they first die and rot and are corrupted, do not produce the ear of grain. Just as therefore, seeing there the grain rotting and dissolving, you do not doubt about the resurrection, but you make for yourself a very clear demonstration; for if it does not remain rotting and being corrupted, it would never rise; so also reason about your own body; when you see corruption, then especially philosophize about the resurrection. For death is nothing other than the removal of corruption henceforth; for death consumes not the body simply, but its corruption. This is possible to see happening also in metallic materials. Those experienced in these things take the gold-bearing earth, and handing it over to the furnace they produce gold, and mixing sand and other material, they made pure glass. Then what the power of fire does, will not the grace of God be able to do, tell me? And who would say these things among those having any sense at all? How he made you in the beginning, consider, and no longer doubt about the resurrection.

choices.english: He made you yourself a craftsman of resurrection
choices.why: δημιουργός means craftsman/creator; God made the human a maker of resurrection through seeds, crafts, and metals, not merely a witness.
In the civic metaphor comparing the body's members to a well-governed city, 'constitution' captures the ordered arrangement; 'way of life' is used later for the angelic conduct.
The compound ἐπενδύομαι means putting on over something already worn, matching Paul's image of not stripping but adding immortality on top.
The passive participle conveys the soul being guided step by step through the senses to knowledge of God, preserving the metaphor of hand-leading.
Death is defined as the removal of corruption, not the destruction of the body; 'removal' preserves the distinction Chrysostom draws.

pass_b_english: But if you want to learn the body's excellence, examine the formation of all its members, their shape, their functions, their harmony with one another. You will see that the constitution of these members toward one another is more precise than any well-governed city whose citizens are all philosophers. And if you pass over all this and bring forward only its corruptible and mortal aspect, we will not lack a defense even from that. For it is clear from this that not only has no harm come from it, but great gain has come to the human race. All the saints who lived with this body displayed that angelic way of life, and it caused them no harm in their course toward virtue. And those who looked toward impiety had no small hindrance in the corruption of the body, keeping them from advancing further in their own lawlessness. For if many people, while clothed in this corruptible and passible body, imagined equality with God and worked hard to wrap such glory around themselves, then if they had not had a passible and corruptible body to expose their weakness, whom would they not have deceived among the more foolish? So when corruption appears as a hindrance even to impiety—which is the furthest limit of wickedness—and provides the saints an opportunity to display the courage of their soul, what pardon could those deserve who slander and abuse it? Nor is this all we can say about it. It has also become for us a cause of the knowledge of God. For since his invisible attributes are perceived through the things he has made, from the creation of the world (Romans 1:20), and faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17), it is clear that the soul, led by the hand through eyes and ears, came to know the God who made it. This is why Paul loves it and cries out, saying, "We do not want to be unclothed, but to put on over it immortality" (2 Corinthians 5:4). And do not tell me, "How can the body rise again and become incorruptible?" When God's power is at work, do not ask how. And why do I speak only of God? He made you yourself to become a craftsman of resurrection—in seeds, in crafts, and in metallic materials. For seeds, unless they first die and rot and decay, do not produce the ear of grain. So when you see the grain rotting and dissolving, you do not doubt the resurrection; you make it a very clear proof for yourself. For unless it remains rotting and decaying, it would never rise. Think the same way about your own body: when you see corruption, then especially reflect on the resurrection. For death is nothing other than the removal of corruption. Death does not consume the body itself, but its corruption. You can see this happening with metallic materials as well. Those experienced in these things take gold-bearing earth, hand it over to the furnace, and produce gold. They mix sand and other material and make pure glass. Tell me then: what the power of fire does, will the grace of God not be able to do? Who among those with any sense at all would say that? Consider how he made you in the beginning, and no longer doubt the resurrection.

problems.quote: For it is clear from the following that not only has no harm come from this
problems.source_quote: Ὅτι γὰρ οὐ μόνον οὐδεμία γέγονεν ἐντεῦθεν ἡ βλάβη, ἀλλὰ καὶ πολὺ τὸ κέρδος τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων, δῆλον ἐκεῖθεν
problems.why: Source says 'clear from there' (ἐκεῖθεν), referring to what precedes; English says 'from the following,' reversing the reference.
problems.fix: For it is clear from this that not only has no harm come from it, but great gain has come to the human race.
problems.ruling: ἐκεῖθεν means 'from there,' referring back; 'from the following' reverses temporal reference, misleading reader.

problems.quote: And why do I speak of God?
problems.source_quote: Καὶ τί λέγω ἐπὶ Θεοῦ; Σὲ δημιουργὸν αὐτὸν ἐποίησεν ἀναστάσεως γενέσθαι
problems.why: Source says 'He made you a craftsman of resurrection' — God made the listener a craftsman; English drops 'you' as object, obscuring agency.
problems.fix: And why do I speak only of God? He made you yourself a craftsman of resurrection.
problems.ruling: Σὲ is explicit accusative 'you'; English 'He made you yourself' garbles to 'He made you yourself a craftsman,' but 'you' as object of ἐποίησεν is lost, obscuring God made the listener a craftsman.

problems.quote: For if it does not remain rotting and decaying, it would never rise
problems.source_quote: ἂν γὰρ μὴ μείνῃ σηπόμενος μηδὲ φθειρόμενος, οὐκ ἂν ἀνασταίη ποτέ
problems.why: Greek says 'if it does NOT remain rotting, it would NOT rise'—English omits the double negative logic.
problems.fix: For unless it remains rotting and decaying, it would never rise
problems.ruling: Source has μὴ μείνῃ...οὐκ ἂν ἀνασταίη: 'if it does NOT remain rotting, it would NOT rise.' English reverses the logic.

last_rejected.quote: keeping them from advancing further in their own lawlessness
last_rejected.source_quote: πρὸς τὸ μὴ ποῤῥωτέρω προελθεῖν τῆς οἰκείας παρανομίας
last_rejected.why: English makes body corruption the agent 'keeping them,' but Greek has τοῦ σώματος τὴν φθορὰν as the hindrance itself, not as active keeper. The syntax is 'had no small hindrance in the corruption of the body, toward not advancing further'—the hindrance is the object they had, not an agent. English 'keeping them' adds agency not in source.
last_rejected.fix: they had no small hindrance in the body's corruption, to keep them from advancing further in their lawlessness
last_rejected.ruling: πρὸς τὸ μὴ ποῤῥωτέρω προελθεῖν = purpose/result; 'keeping them from' fairly renders the hindrance's effect.

last_rejected.quote: then if they had not had a passible and corruptible body to expose their weakness
last_rejected.source_quote: εἰ μὴ παθητὸν εἶχον τὸ σῶμα καὶ φθαρτὸν, ἐλέγχον αὐτῶν τὴν ἀσθένειαν
last_rejected.why: English conditional 'then if' misrepresents the Greek: εἰ μὴ = 'if not,' a contrary-to-fact condition about past, but the English 'then if' makes it a present hypothetical consequence of previous clause, not the unfulfilled condition it is. Should be 'if they had not had' as apodosis to implied protasis.
last_rejected.fix: if they had not had a passible and corruptible body, which exposed their weakness
last_rejected.ruling: English 'if they had not had' correctly renders εἰ μὴ εἶχον; 'then' just links to prior clause.

last_rejected.quote: what pardon could those deserve who slander and abuse it
last_rejected.source_quote: τίνος ἂν τύχοιεν συγγνώμης οἱ διαβάλλοντες αὐτὸ καὶ κακίζοντες
last_rejected.why: τύχοιεν = 'obtain, receive,' not 'deserve.' The question is what pardon would they receive/obtain, not what they deserve. 'Deserve' changes modality from possibility/result to merit.
last_rejected.fix: what pardon would those who slander and abuse it receive
last_rejected.ruling: τυγχάνω in rhetorical question = 'obtain/deserve'; 'deserve' is normal English for such idiom.

last_rejected.quote: We do not want to be unclothed, but to put on over it immortality
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ θέλομεν αὐτὸ ἐκδύσασθαι, ἀλλ' ἐπενδύσασθαι αὐτῷ τὴν ἀθανασίαν
last_rejected.why: ἐπενδύσασθαι αὐτῷ = 'to put on OVER IT,' but English 'put on over it immortality' is awkward. More critically: αὐτὸ in first clause is 'it' (the body), but English 'be unclothed' loses the object—we do not want to strip IT off. The 'it' is the body, and 'be unclothed' is middle voice but with object. English 'to be unclothed' sounds like passive or intransitive, losing 'it.'
last_rejected.fix: We do not want to strip it off, but to put on immortality over it
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκδύσασθαι αὐτό = 'unclothed from it'; 'be unclothed' captures middle sense; 'over it' renders αὐτῷ dative.

last_rejected.quote: For unless it remains rotting and decaying, it would never rise
last_rejected.source_quote: ἂν γὰρ μὴ μείνῃ σηπόμενος μηδὲ φθειρόμενος, οὐκ ἂν ἀνασταίη ποτέ
last_rejected.why: English 'it remains rotting and decaying' suggests continuing state, but Greek μείνῃ σηπόμενος = 'remain IN A STATE OF rotting,' i.e., undergo the process. The logic is: unless it undergoes rotting/decaying, it won't rise. English 'remains rotting' is slightly off—'remains' suggests staying in that state, but the Greek means 'unless it endures/becomes rotting.' However, this is close. More critically: the subject is the grain/seed (κόκκος), but English 'it' refers back to 'the grain'—correct.
last_rejected.fix: For unless it undergoes rotting and decaying, it would never rise
last_rejected.ruling: μείνῃ σηπόμενος = 'remain rotting'; 'remains rotting and decaying' is accurate for the process.
